This is not due to crisis per-se. Mario Draghi recently actually lead this report commissioned by EU itself to investigate why GDP growth was so slow in EU and it has very little to do with the 2008 financial crisis or monetary policy.

TL;DR from this official investigation:

First, the overarching reason is that in EU there was slow to none productivity growth. Monetary policy can affect GDP in short term but over decades real GDP per capita is pretty much determined by productivity growth.

However in turn the productivity growth depends on other variables, like investments into R&D.

According to the Draghi’s report to the EU commission the reason for slow EU productivity growth was;

  • weak investment in adapting new technologies. EU spends a considerable sums on research but lot of this money is wasted because every country has its own National programs and there is a lot of double work being done. Moreover, EU has problem with deploying new technologies in businesses.

    In fact the report shows that the biggest factor that accounts for US-EU productivity, and hence also GDP gap, is the US technological sector. In EU we do not have any native tech giants like in US, EU according to the report missed on digital Revolution.

  • a lot of regulations, and even often inconsistent regulations, which make commercialization of new technologies difficult.

  • lack of capital markets. Many startups relocate to US to tap into US capital markets. In EU, especially after UK left, we do not really have many well organized capital markets where firms can raise capital. At least not compared to US.

  • skill gap. EU has a lack of skilled workers needed by businesses. There is greater mismatch on labor markets compared to US. This is according to the report mainly due to education. This is reinforced by aging population. I dont remember if this was also mentioned in the report itself, but EU also has problem with attracting high skilled migrants compared to US.

  • De-globalization. The report argues EU was especially hard hit by recent de-globalization trend.

  • inconsistent industrial policy. EU does not properly cooperate on industrial policy and EU countries often pursue various inconsistent industrial policies.

  • high energy costs. EU economy is dependent on hydrocarbons that it cannot produce on its own. Traditionally, EU got its hydrocarbons from Russia, but recently that became problematic. Hence the report also argues that to in order to restore economic growth EU will have to decarbonize. US is less exposed to these problems because US is one of the worlds biggest hydrocarbon producers. Hence US energy costs were much less affected by Russian invasion.

I think the above are all the main points identified in the EU report.

Also notably the report doesn’t mention monetary policy much. There is only 1 mention of it in an endnote and it is in connection with decarbonization. The 2008 crisis is also only mentioned twice but once with connection of falling unemployment (which is not bad for economy) and once in connection to gap between private saving/investment which opened between US and EU (in EU people started to invest less). However, it’s unclear what caused this and the report doesn’t attribute this to the 2008 crisis.

Generally, if the hypothesis is that is was due to the worse recovery from the 2008 crisis is true, you would expect that there would be constant gap between US and EU that started at 2008. However, what we see is that there are opening scissors between EU and US. Demand side shocks (e.g. the 2008 crisis) and monetary policy do not have much power over long run growth. The 2008 crisis could only be responsible to the extent it might have contributed to some of the above cases (e.g. anecdotally according to WEF slow/de-globalization started after 2008 crisis, although, it really accelerated during Covid and Russian invasion. Trump's and Biden's trade wars also contributed).

A crisis that the report mentioned the most is the ‘energy crisis’ in EU. Which refers to the fact that EU has consistently for long periods of time very high energy costs (if you are person living in EU you might know that energy costs are high but your personal bill is still indirectly subsidized by government. Business face much worse energy costs than you as a person). This is a supply side shock that can affect long run growth.
query:
Why has the US recovered from the financial crisis much more successfully than Europe?

When looking at the GDP and GDP/capita graphs for the US and EU since 2008, there appears to be a clear divergence. What caused this? Is it due to better American fiscal / monetary policy? Another possible conclusion is brain drain - a European with any talent or ambition will be much more successful in the US, but I can't really think of anything else.

On the night of Saturday 19 December 1942, there was a fire at a store in Hayes, Middlesex. The store, the responsibility of the Office of Works, contained a large amount of furniture but in addition it contained the census records for England & Wales for 1931, that is the whole of the schedules, enumeration books and plans. They were all completely destroyed.

The fire was not caused by enemy action and the civil servant from the General Register Office who visited the site a few days later was bemused as to how a fire "achieved such dimensions in a store in which special hydrants had been fitted and was said to have been in charge of a fire guard of 6 paid firewatchers" and that it is "a mystery which will need investigation".

He reported that he and his colleague "are both satisfied that it would be useless to attempt any sort of salvage operation; we are leaving the Office of Works to clear and dispose of the debris in any way they think desirable".

1911census.org.uk has more information on it.
query:
Do any fragments of the 1931 census of England & Wales survive?

It is a well known fact that the 1931 census of England and Wales was destroyed by a fire during the Second World War. However, did any fragments of this census survive at all? Were both the household schedules and the enumerators' summary books completely destroyed?

Looking over the various sources, it appears that this was a modification of a process invented by American scientist Samuel Kistler in the early 1960's, and already commercialized for niche applications that really needed stronger glass by Corning. Their product line Gorilla Glass is these days mostly known for its use in cellphone screens.

A lot of the public talk about what happened appears to be from the East German point of view, and reads rather like the words of an author insisting their readers are dumb for not understanding the genius of their writing, or a software developer insisting users who keep finding bugs are dumb and using it wrong. One thing that seems really hard for new creators to get over is the idea that their consumers are their ultimate judge. East Germans of course were quite new to the concept of trying to create and market products for Capitalist free markets, and appear to have taken the attitude that the market was dumb for not recognizing their genius.

In particular, it appears that the problem with the East German product was that it wasn't trying to compete in these niche spaces where tougher glass was a major market driver, and instead was trying to compete in the market space of mass-produced drinking glasses. I suppose this could be spun as drinking glass manufacturers not wanting to lower their own sales, but it would be a silly gripe because no commercial entity wants to do that. Its ultimately the consumer that drives the market, and in the aggregate the western free market clearly didn't care enough about their glasses breaking slightly less to justify the extra cost.

I was able to find a somewhat scientific survey of the breakage rate of consumer glasses, and its not really all that high. Like an annual failure rate of 0.167, which I believe means you can expect to have to replace a drinking glass after about 6 years of use.

That's roughly the lifetime of some large dog breeds. For a lot of people, particularly those without a lot of excess money to throw around (people who have limited funds, and have to both buy new drinking glasses and pay for food and rent this month with those funds), that's going to be long enough.

For those who do have a lot of money to throw around, if they are going to pay "luxury" prices for something simple like drinking glasses, they are probably going to want something that looks like a luxury product. These glasses, perhaps betraying their creators' socialist design aesthetic, looked, well ... common. Functional.

There's another little-reported issue with these glasses. While they can be dropped a few times before breaking (this tester found 5 for the one glass they tested), when they do break its far more of a problem to clean up:

While the Superfest glass is by far more durable than normal glass, when they shatter – the burst into a million fine pieces and are a total nightmare to clean up. I’m not sure if it’s because of their potassium chloride coating or because they are made to be super thin, my advice is to not drop them.

I probably needn't point out this is disappointing advice, if you spent a premium on these because they are less likely to break when dropped.

So the essential issue here was that, when you factor in things like cost, aesthetics, and and breakage cleanup, these glasses were not objectively better than the other available options for all users. Perhaps the East German designers and their marketers could have tweaked their product and their marketing strategy to better find their products a market niche, but for whatever reason, it doesn't appear that was done.
query:
Why was "superfest" glass unsuccessful outside East Germany?

Inventors in communist East Germany invented a glass that was less likely to break. It was called superfest (super-strong) glass and was used for mass-producing beer glasses and other drinking glasses. See e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superfest.

It was not successful outside East Germany and the story goes that people in "capitalist" countries did not want to sell something that does not break because it reduces their sales in the future. I am unconvinced by this reasoning: If I could license a patent for super-strong glass and produce beer glasses that very rarely break, I could probably make a lot of money by selling them to pubs and restaurants. And even if the market is saturated in five or ten years, I would probably have earned a lot by then.

So I wonder: What is the real reason nobody wanted that glass? Was the production of the glass expensive? Did it have some other detrimental properties? A bad look or feel?

Good evidence would e.g. be manufacturing costs of the superfest glass compared to normal glass, or first-hand opinions given by glass manufacturers. Evidence could also be if there was a similar product in the Western world which failed to be successful.

A good review addressing the question is:

  • Lombardi, M. A., Heavner, T. P., & Jefferts, S. R. (2007). NIST primary frequency standards and the realization of the SI second. NCSLI Measure, 2(4), 74-89.

Compare also the wikipedia entry on Ephemeris time.

The detailed story here is complicated, and there are numerous aspects of the question that do not directly map to the historical development. Specifically, the comparison of ephemeris time was not centered around 1967, but around 1957, and was not based on the mean solar day. It turns out that measuring the moon's motion is more precise than measuring the sun's.

The detailed measurements comparing Ephemeris Time with Cesium transition frequency was conducted and documented in:

  • Markowitz, W., Hall, R. G., Essen, L., & Parry, J. V. L. (1958). Frequency of cesium in terms of ephemeris time. Physical Review Letters, 1(3), 105.

1967 was not a hard transition from a mean solar day standard. Instead there was a transition period, considerations spanned the 1950's leading to a definition in 1960 of the second as:

the second is the fraction 1/31,556,985.974 7 of the tropical year for 1900 January 0 at 12 hours ephemeris time

Clearly the notion of mean day had already been replaced with a fixed period at a fixed date. This however should be seen as part of a transition towards an atomic clock-based norm.

Discussions of the standard committees were chronicled by Terrien. A longer form exposition of the period can be found in where the ultimate adoption of the 1967 is already strongly anticipated:

  • Terrien, J. (1965). Scientific metrology on the international plane and the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures. Metrologia, 1(1), 15.

Here we find an explanation for the transition to the 1960 definition:

The unit of time of the physicists, the second, has been defined as the fraction 1/86,400 of the mean solar day. Determination of the mean solar day is not a simple matter, but, again, atronomers [sic] could do it by observing the apparent angular movements of celestial bodies caused by the rotation of the Earth around its axis. But it was discovered that this rotation is slowing down, and, in addition, it varies in an erratic manner, as proved by observation of the Moon, or of Mercury, or, more recently, by comparison of astronomical time with quartz clocks. Astronomers then chose to define the second in terms of the year, instead of the day, that is to use as a standard the duration of one revolution of the Earth around the Sun, when numerous corrections have been applied. Even the duration of the year, the tropical year to be more precise, changes slowly by a known amount.
query:
Question about the history of the definition of the second in SI

This question is about specifically:

Why, in 1967, did the 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), choose 9192631770 cycles of radiation (corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the cesium-133 atom) to define a second and not a value that was perfect match to $\frac{1}{86400}$ solar day at that time?.

With that many cycles defining a second, at that time, circa 1965-1967, the mean solar day was about 2 or 2.5 ms longer than 86400 SI seconds. Why didn't they define the second to be 9192631982 cycles of this same cesium-133 radiation?

At what year (and I don't mean in the very recent past, but when atomic clocks were a new thing) was the mean solar day exactly 86400 SI seconds? What was the historical basis for the difference in the redefinition of a second to be consistent with the previous definition at that time?
